title: Early life exposure to house dust mite allergen prevents experimental allergic asthma requiring mitochondrial H(2)O(2).
ehr_evidence: The study utilized wild-type and MCAT transgenic mice purchased from Jackson Laboratories and housed at the University of Pittsburgh.
summary: Experimental mouse study demonstrating that early-life low-dose house dust mite (HDM) exposure induces airway tolerance via mitochondrial H2O2 production in lung dendritic cells, preventing allergic asthma.
key_findings: Early-life exposure to low-dose HDM (0.5 µg) at 2 weeks prevented airway inflammation and mucus upon challenge at 6 weeks, whereas high-dose HDM (5 µg) did not.
Low-dose HDM reduced BAL fluid cellularity and significantly decreased IL-13- and IL-5-producing CD4+ T cells compared to the inflammation group.
WT tolerant mice showed a 50% decrease in total lung dendritic cell numbers compared to naïve mice.
MCAT mice (mitochondrial H2O2-depleted) failed to establish tolerance and harbored approximately 3-fold more total DCs and cDC1/cDC2 subsets than WT tolerant mice.
Depletion of mitochondrial H2O2 abolished tolerance, resulting in increased airway hyperreactivity, eosinophil-dominated inflammation, and elevated serum IgE levels.
RT-qPCR revealed 2-fold higher S100a4:Irf8 and 1.5-fold higher Irf4:Irf8 expression ratios in DCs from tolerant MCAT mice compared to tolerant WT mice.
captured_features: lung histology inflammation and mucus scores
lung tissue cytokine and gene expression (Ifng, Il13, Il17a, Irf4, Irf8, S100a4)
flow cytometry quantification of T cell subsets and DC/macrophage populations
population: 2-week-old and 6-week-old wild-type and MCAT transgenic mice
limitations: Inability to assess DC functional capacity using T cells with TCR specificity for HDM antigen Der p 1.
Findings are derived from a murine model, limiting direct translation to human clinical settings.
